P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: Yes, under exchange control. Resident individuals' 'foreign earned income' is exempt from Exchange Control Regulations 6 and 7 only where earned on approved foreign assets or for services rendered to non-residents WHILE PHYSICALLY ABROAD (SARB AD Manual B.17(A)). For services rendered from inside South Africa, the general rule applies: individuals holding foreign currency outside South Africa must offer it for sale to an Authorised Dealer within 30 days of becoming entitled to it, unless exempted. Individuals may, however, keep legitimate foreign earned income in a foreign currency account with an Authorised Dealer (P2). Inward foreign-earned funds are reported under BOP category 210.

sources.title: Currency and Exchanges Manual for Authorised Dealers (2026), B.17(A)
sources.quote: Private individuals (natural persons) resident in South Africa are exempted from the provisions of Regulations 6 and 7 in respect of foreign earned income with effect from 1997 -07-01 (i.e. income earned on approved foreign assets or in respect of services rendered to non-residents while physically abroad), with the exception of the proceeds of merchandise exports, which must be repatriated to South Africa within 30 days from the date of becoming entitled thereto.

sources.title: Currency and Exchanges Guidelines for Individuals (1/2026), 3.7.1
sources.quote: Individuals and foreign nationals who are holders of foreign currencies outside South Africa must, unless exempted elsewhere in terms of the provisions of this document, offer to sell their holdings to an Authorised Dealer within 30 days from the date of becoming entitled thereto.

P1_fx_receipts.notes: The 'physically abroad' qualifier means remote freelancers working from SA are not covered by the B.17(A) exemption. Confirm treatment with an Authorised Dealer. The 30-day sale duty in 3.7.1 refers to holdings OUTSIDE SA. Funds deposited in a local foreign currency account (P2) are within the system.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes. SARB permits individuals to conduct a foreign currency account with an Authorised Dealer (and/or a foreign bank account) for travel, foreign investment, legitimate foreign earned income and foreign inheritance. CFC (Customer Foreign Currency) accounts proper are for legal persons, e.g. entities providing services in SA to non-residents.

P4_paypal.question: Can residents receive money via PayPal?
P4_paypal.answer: Yes. PayPal lists South Africa as 'Send, receive, and withdraw' and covers ZA in its merchant fee schedule. Withdrawals go through the FNB Withdraw Service with PayPal, which moves PayPal funds to an FNB account or any linked South African bank account (up to 4–6 business days). FNB states withdrawals must be made within 30 days of receipt, for exchange-control compliance (secondary summary; see notes).

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: No company is needed. A sole proprietorship, owned and operated by a natural person, is the simplest form and has no existence separate from the owner, so its income goes on the owner's personal return. As soon as a person commences a business, they must register as a taxpayer with SARS (eFiling or service centre) within 21 business days of becoming liable. Business income makes the owner a provisional taxpayer.

sources.title: Tax Guide for Small Businesses 2025/2026
sources.quote: A sole proprietorship is a business that is owned and operated by a natural person and is the simplest form of business type. The business itself has no existence separate from the owner who is called the proprietor

sources.title: Tax Guide for Small Businesses 2025/2026 — registration
sources.quote: The person must register within 21 business days after becoming liable for any normal tax or becoming liable to submit any return.

L1_registration.notes: CIPC (cipc.co.za) timed out; registering a sole proprietorship with CIPC is not required (no legal personality).

L2_tax_id.question: Tax ID: who needs one, how to get it?
L2_tax_id.answer: The SARS income tax reference number, obtained by registering as a taxpayer on SARS eFiling, the SARS MobiApp or at a service centre, within 21 business days of becoming liable.

sources.title: Tax Guide for Small Businesses 2025/2026
sources.quote: the person is required to register as a taxpayer with the SARS service centre or on SARS eFiling15 to obtain a tax reference number.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Residents (ordinarily resident, or meeting the physical-presence test) are taxed on worldwide income. 2026/27 brackets: 18% up to R245,100, rising through 26%, 31%, 36%, 39% and 41%, to 45% above R1,878,600. Turnover Tax for micro-businesses (2026/27): 0% to R600,000, 1%, 2%, then 3% above R1.4m, for turnover up to R2.3m. NOT available to natural persons with more than 20% of receipts from 'professional services' (which include consulting, IT, accounting, law and others).

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: VAT is 15%. Compulsory registration threshold: R2.3m of taxable supplies per year from 1 April 2026 (voluntary from R120,000). This is proposed in the DRAFT 2026 Rates Bill and not yet promulgated as of Sept 2026, but SARS already applies it to new registrations and deregistrations from 1 April 2026; the previous statutory figure was R1m. Services supplied to non-residents are zero-rated under VAT Act s.11(2)(l), subject to exclusions (e.g. where the recipient is in SA when services are rendered) and documentary proof.

sources.quote: From 1 April 2026: The compulsory registration threshold applies when the total value of taxable supplies exceeds R2.3 million per annum (increased from R1 million).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA), enforced by the Information Regulator. Public and private bodies, including individuals (sole proprietors) and small businesses that process personal information, must register their Information Officer (and deputies) with the Regulator via the eServices portal. Information Officers may take up duties only after registration (s.55). Security compromises are reported via the same portal.

sources.title: POPIA — s.55
sources.quote: Registering Information Officers The Information Officers are required, in terms of Section 55(2) of POPIA, to take up their duties only after being registered with the Regulator.

sources.title: Home — Registration of Information Officers
sources.quote: In accordance with the stipulations laid out in Section 55 of the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013 (POPIA), Information Officers must assume their duties only after the responsible party has registered them with the Regulator.

L5_data_protection.notes: The Regulator's FAQ reportedly says non-registration is not itself an offence, but the head of the body is liable (search summary; not captured).

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: Electronic Communications and Transactions Act 25 of 2002, s.44: in electronic transactions a consumer may cancel without reason or penalty within 7 days of receiving goods, or of concluding a services agreement. The only charge allowed is the direct cost of returning goods, and prepaid amounts must be refunded within 30 days. Statutory exclusions apply (e.g. financial services, auctions, foodstuffs, services begun with consent before the period ends).

L6_consumer_ecommerce.notes: The s.42 exclusions list was seen in summaries only.

L7_incentives.question: Legal incentives / tax holidays / special zones relevant to small digital businesses
L7_incentives.answer: (1) Turnover Tax: 0% on the first R600,000 and max 3% for micro-businesses up to R2.3m, but excluded for those with more than 20% of receipts from professional services such as IT and consulting (L3). (2) Higher VAT thresholds from 1 Apr 2026 (applied administratively; L4). (3) Zero-rating of services exported to non-residents (L4). (4) Special Economic Zones offer a 15% corporate rate for qualifying companies (not individuals).

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Send, receive, and withdraw'). (7) Card payments on your own site through Paystack (a Stripe company). Stripe lists this country under its extended network. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
